findings: The preserved source only names the kth-missing-positive problem and records binary search as a technical entity; it does not preserve the complete array and k constraints. The candidate explicitly marks strictly increasing positive input and k>=1 as its executable contract instead of attributing those details to the source.

Within that contract, missing(i)=arr[i]-(i+1) is monotone, so the first index whose cumulative missing count reaches k is a valid lower-bound target. The candidate derives the final value lo+k rather than presenting it as a memorized formula.
The displayed Java block is a complete compilable class and matches the separately executed fixture implementation.

The deterministic fixture passes the standard internal case, an answer after the array tail, an answer before the first element, empty input, multiple gaps, a long result beyond int range, null rejection and non-positive-k rejection.
The candidate states the O(log n) core query cost while explicitly explaining that defensive O(n) validation of the sorted-positive precondition would change end-to-end complexity.

Follow-ups cover the missing-count formula, monotonicity, lo+k derivation, tail behavior, invalid ordering and the O(n) alternative; no project experience, exact platform identity, or unpreserved constraints are fabricated.
No uncovered source variant, unsupported source attribution, coding hard failure, or semantic blocker remains. Formal promotion remains subject to repository promotion and real-review policy.
